text: During decoding, each token contributes a key and a value to the KV cache.
The next query attends to the stored keys, then mixes the stored values.
As requests grow at different speeds, where should all these KV entries live?
Imagine reserving 12 token slots per request, before its final length is known.
Instead, allocate fixed-size blocks on demand. Here, one block holds four tokens.
Only a request’s last block can have unused slots: at most B − 1 per sequence.
Logical blocks preserve token order. Physical blocks can live anywhere in the pool.
For token 6 with B = 4: logical block = floor(6 / 4) = 1, offset = 2.
The table maps logical block 1 to physical block 2. The token offset stays 2.
The attention kernel follows the block table to read the request’s keys and values.
Each key produces a score. All valid scores share one softmax normalization.
Mix the values with these weights. Paging changes addresses, not the attention formula.
A six-token request owns two blocks. Its last block still has room.
Tokens 6 and 7 fill existing space. No new physical block is needed.
Token 8 crosses a block boundary. Allocate a free block and extend the table.
When this request finishes, its unshared blocks return to the pool for reuse.
Two continuations can share the same prefix blocks instead of duplicating their KV data.
If A appends to a shared partial block, first copy that block to a new physical block.
A writes token 6 into its private copy. B’s cache is untouched; the full prefix stays shared.
PagedAttention combines block-based storage, address translation, and safe KV-cache sharing.
